interactions.summary: Jiang declines to analyze Japan's new prime minister in detail, but says the China-Japan rupture is already serious enough that China-based workers have received warnings that Japan is unsafe and politically risky to visit.
Danny starts to wrap the interview, asks whether there is anything major they missed, and Jiang agrees they have effectively covered the whole map.
Danny asks where listeners can follow Jiang's work, and Jiang directs them to his Predictive History Substack for geopolitical analysis.
Danny reopens the substance at the last minute, asking whether Jiang still expects an Iranian attack around December, while noting that Trita Parsi had pointed to December as well.

Jiang answers that the Iran timetable has been pushed back, briefly points Danny toward David Miller on Pax Judaica, and then argues that Iran is not passive but strategically waiting for the American empire to become sufficiently distracted, wounded, or internally chaotic before striking.

speaker_notes.note: Jiang says he does not follow 'Southeast Asia politics' even though the immediate question is about Japan. The surrounding answer makes clear that he is declining detailed Japanese domestic-political analysis while still commenting on the broader China-Japan security atmosphere.
The David Miller recommendation and Pax Judaica attribution are a brief digression inside Jiang's Iran answer, not a separate new topic turn.
The transcript's 'general Salamini' is an ASR corruption of Qasem Soleimani. Preserve Jiang's point about Trump's assassination of the Iranian general without normalizing the quote text inside refs.

claims.claim: Jiang says he is not tracking Japanese domestic politics closely, but from his position in China he sees the current China-Japan rupture as serious enough that workers have been told Japan is unsafe and politically dangerous to visit.
He cites an unofficial social mechanism behind that warning by saying that if a person working in China goes to Japan now, the trip can leave a political black mark on them.
Jiang identifies his Predictive History Substack as the main place where he publishes his geopolitical analysis.
Jiang revises the earlier December attack expectation by saying the Iran timetable has been pushed back.
He credits British academic David Miller as a major source for the Pax Judaica framework he has been using in the interview and recommends Danny interview him directly.

Jiang argues that Iran's current restraint should be read as strategic patience rather than stealth, passivity, or naivete, because toppling the American empire requires waiting for a moment of weakness.

He says Iran's best strike window would come when America is overextended in Ukraine and convulsed by internal political chaos, giving Tehran a chance to land a decisive blow while the hegemon is off balance.
claims.temporal_scope: Conditional future war scenario stated on 2025-11-30.

claims.claim: Jiang grounds Iran's motive in accumulated humiliation, saying Trump's killing of Soleimani was a major loss of face that helps explain why Tehran still wants to retaliate but is waiting for the right time.
claims.temporal_scope: Present-tense motive analysis tied to prior events, stated on 2025-11-30.

signature_moments.moment: The China-Japan rift is rendered not as an abstract diplomatic chill but as a practical stigma: go to Japan now and you carry a black mark back with you.
signature_moments.source_phrase: if you go to Japan, there'll be a black mark on you
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It converts a broad geopolitical tension into a lived disciplinary image and gives the East Asia pressure a concrete social texture.

signature_moments.moment: Iran is imagined as a boxer facing a gorilla, waiting for the larger beast to wobble before throwing the one punch that matters.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's sharpest strategic metaphor and it compresses Jiang's whole theory of Iranian patience into one memorable combat image.

signature_moments.moment: The right strike is not constant resistance but opportunism: wait for imperial distraction, hobbling, and civil chaos, then hit hard.
signature_moments.source_phrase: when he's distracted, when he's a bit hobbled, when he's a bit hurt
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It turns Jiang's Iran reading into a compact method for how weaker powers survive against a hegemon they cannot defeat head-on.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's name for the Israeli-centered successor order he has been discussing throughout the interview, here explicitly attributed in part to British academic David Miller's analysis of Zionism.
The honor-political injury Jiang uses to explain why Iran may delay retaliation without abandoning it: humiliation can intensify motive while still requiring careful timing.

chronology_notes.note: On 2025-11-30 Jiang explicitly walks back the earlier December-Iran-strike timing and replaces it with a strategic-patience model: retaliation remains possible, but only after deeper American distraction or internal crisis.

uncertainty_notes.note: Jiang declines detailed Japan domestic-political analysis here, so the packet should not infer a substantive view of the new prime minister beyond the broader China-Japan security tension he does describe.
The David Miller mention is source attribution inside Jiang's own framework, not an independent verification of the Pax Judaica thesis.
The American civil-war, impeachment, and strike-window sequence is a hypothetical scenario Jiang uses to illustrate timing logic, not a confirmed future event.
